    Injectable peptides for hair growth: legal status and evidence.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    Research-use shops sell BPC-157, GHK-Cu copper peptide and TB-500 in vials for hair. None is FDA approved for any use, and we found no trial in people that shows any of them grows hair.1

    Which injectable peptides are sold for hair?

    The hair vials we see at research-use shops are BPC-157, GHK-Cu copper peptide and TB-500. They come as a powder in a vial, meant to be mixed with water and injected. The label says they are for research, not for people.

    They are not approved medicines. A medicine needs FDA approval first: its maker sends trial data, and the FDA checks that the benefits outweigh the risks.3 Nobody has done that for these peptides.

    What is their FDA status?

    From our database, with the FDA page behind each one:

    • BPC-157: Not approved for any use.1
    • GHK-Cu copper peptide: Not approved for any use.1
    • TB-500: Not approved for any use.1

    The FDA lists BPC-157 among the substances that may be risky in pharmacy-made medicines: it may set off an immune reaction when given some ways, and there is little or no safety information on it in people.4

    In July 2026 the FDA's advisory committee on pharmacy compounding reviewed BPC-157 and TB-500: FDA advisory committee reviewed it for compounding on 23 Jul 2026; FDA proposed not to allow it.2 Our guide Is BPC-157 legal? explains what that review means.

    Is there any evidence they grow hair?

    Not in people, as far as we could find. The hair study quoted for copper peptides was done on follicles in a dish, with AHK-Cu, a close relative of GHK-Cu.5 The studies on BPC-157 are in animals and cells.4

    A study in a dish or in mice tells you what a substance does to cells. It does not tell you what an injection does to your hair, or what it does to the rest of you.

    A price per mg does not tell you either. It says nothing about what is in the vial: a lab report covers one batch, tested once, and only if a lab outside the shop did the test. Our guide on how to read a COA shows what to look for. Our best peptides for hair growth guide puts these vials next to serums, biotin and the approved options.

    What has the FDA said to the shops?

    A warning letter is the FDA's formal notice, not a court ruling.6 Our guide on what an FDA warning letter means explains what follows one.

    What do the approved options cost at online clinics?

    Finasteride 1 mg is FDA approved for hair loss in men.7 Minoxidil on the scalp is approved too, and sold without a prescription.8 Minoxidil tablets are a blood pressure medicine; for hair, a prescriber decides whether they fit you.9

    Pharmacy-made mixes, such as finasteride and minoxidil in one capsule, are not themselves FDA-approved products.10 A clinic with an FDA letter is still listed: the letter is public record.

    None of this is medical advice. A doctor or dermatologist can tell you which option fits your hair loss.
